AAMIR. Assalam-o-Alaikum. Our paper is Prompts Are Not Policies. An AI agent manages network traffic: it can allow, block or slow down a flow. We test whether rules written in its prompt are enough, or whether it needs a small code check before every action.

AAMIR. Agents now act through tools, and their rules usually sit in the prompt, so obeying them is the model's choice. In a network, one wrong action hits every packet of a flow, and the flow's type comes from a classifier that can be wrong. That is our research problem, on the right.

AAMIR. Earlier work either adds a second model to review each action, which costs extra calls, or runs code rules before a tool executes. Both are mostly tested on customer service, web and code tasks, and both trust their input facts. The network-agent studies we reviewed do not let an agent act on single flows.

AAMIR. We ask four questions: how often the agent breaks the rules with only a prompt, how much a gate prevents, whether telling it why it failed helps, and what still gets through. The agent answers each scenario once, and we replay that same answer under every condition.

AAMIR. A Random Forest labels each flow. The agent sees that label and the request, and proposes one JSON action. The gate runs the four checks at the bottom; if any fails, nothing is executed. Ibrahim will cover the setup and results.

IBRAHIM. We used the ISCXVPN2016 encrypted-traffic dataset. The Random Forest reaches 87.7% accuracy. The agent is Llama 3.2 3B running on a laptop. The gate is plain Python, checked on all 77,035 combinations of tool, class and rate. We built 100 scenarios: normal requests, forbidden requests and injected notes.

IBRAHIM. With only the prompt, 30 actions broke the policy, and the agent obeyed all 25 forbidden requests. With the gate, 6 remain, injections drop to zero, and we keep 97.9% of normal tasks. Each check takes 3.6 microseconds.

IBRAHIM. Sending the rejection reason back recovered 4 tasks but created one new violation: the agent found an action the gate accepts but the real rule forbids. All 6 remaining violations come from wrong classifier labels; with correct labels there are none.

IBRAHIM. The base papers use different benchmarks, so we compare effect size and cost. Our gate cuts violations by 24 points with no extra model calls, while an AI verifier needs up to 2.2 times as many calls. It works because our policy is a simple lookup.

IBRAHIM. In short: a prompt is not enforcement; a small code gate is, but it is only as good as the labels it reads. Next we want bigger models, multi-step tasks and better handling of uncertain labels. Thank you, we are happy to take questions.
